![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/58ebecdd8284dff6e807465f29c890bd87ec763896242cbff2bd1d18a4728f49.png)

The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of a continuous function $y=f(x)$, is given above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y=f(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there are two critical points: 

$\,$ $x=-2\,$ and $\,x=3$ 

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-2)$ | $-2$ | $(-2,3)$ | $3$ | $(3,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical points. Consider the vertical lines $x=-2$ and $x=3.$

- We choose an arbitrary point on the vertical line $x=-2.$

- Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(-2,3),$ the point at $x=3$ must be higher than the point at $x=-2.$

So, we draw it as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/ac3ad854bdef4e5c7011a81a14da722cef44657e8024a39533179513589d0867.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-\infty ,-2)$ and increasing $↗$ on $(-2,3)$, the graph of $f(x)$ goes up to the left and to the right of $x=-2.$

- Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(-2,3)$ and decreasing $↘$ on $(3,\infty )$, the graph of $f(x)$ goes down to the left and to the right of $x=3.$

- Furthermore, since ${f}^{′}(x)$ is increasing to the left of $x=1$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)>0$, and, since it is decreasing to the right of $x=1$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)<0.$ So, $x=1$ is an inflection point at which the curve $y=f(x)$ changes from concave up to concave down.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/81870d6d4fbba512d353788dd06062e380baeb672002f150b2c54eeac73a1bd7.png)

- Finally, since we are told that our graph must be continuous, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/b243c1cfb9da30100aee5f215e02c5eb11769cef1ba4b2b5b74f2879e8a34e10.png)

**Note:** The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. Any similar graph that's shifted vertically up or down could also be considered a possible $y=f(x).$
